          "text": "## 2.2.3. SolÕent extraction studies\nExtraction and stripping tests were carried out batchwise by contacting suitable volumes of the organic and aqueous phases in a 50-ml centrifuge tube or a 500-ml separatory funnel at ambient temperature (25 ± 0.5 ^∘C). The pH was adjusted by the addition of a concentrated sodium hydroxide solution to the appropriate value. From preliminary extraction experiments with D2EHPA to investigate the influence of contact time, a 30-min period appeared to be sufficient to reach extraction and stripping equilibria of the metal ions, except for the stripping of aluminum, which required about 60 min to achieve equilibrium. The extraction and stripping kinetics of cobalt with TOA were very rapid. The time for reaching extraction equilibrium was less than 5 min, while the stripping occurred almost immediately after the loaded organic phase was contacted with a stripping agent.           "text": "## 3.2. Leaching studies\nThe effect of four variables, viz., HCl concentration, temperature, reaction time and solid-to-liquid ratio on metal leaching was studied.\nThe relationship between the percentages of metals leached and the HCl concentration is shown in Fig. 1. The leaching of metals was found to depend highly on the HCl concentration at [ HCl ] < 2 mol l ^-1. Nearly complete dissolution occurred for all metals when the HCl concentration approached 3 mol 1 ^-1. However, there appeared to be a slight decrease in the percent of the rare earths leached when the HCl concentration exceeded 4 mol 1 ^-1\nFig. 2 illustrates that the leaching of iron is affected significantly by temperature. At low temperature, for instance, at 35 ^ ∘C, the percent leached could only reach about 40%, whereas this value would be increased with the increase in temperature, reaching completion at 95 ^ ∘C. It appears that the leach efficiency of nickel was less dependent on temperature at < 65 ^ ∘C, where the percent of nickel leached was kept at approximately 87 %. However, when the temperature was allowed to continue to rise, the leaching of nickel increased. Almost total dissolution was accomplished at 95 ^ ∘C.. The leaching of other metals was far less dependent on temperature over the temperature range examined. Essentially complete leaching could be achieved at 35 ^ ∘C for cobalt, rare earths and aluminum and at 55 ^ ∘C for zinc and manganese.\nThe time dependency of the leaching of metals with 2 M HCl solution at 95 ^ ∘C is given in Fig. 3. Apparently, the leaching of cobalt, aluminum, manganese and rare earths proceeded very rapidly, reaching completion in less than 15 min for aluminum and manganese and less than 30 min for cobalt and rare earths. On the other hand, the relatively slow leaching of iron, zinc and nickel, especially the latter, was observed. The complete leaching was achieved in about 1, 2 and 2.5 h for iron, zinc and nickel, respectively.\nThe effect of the weight of scrap on the leaching of metals is shown in Table 2 in terms of the percent recovery of metals in the leach liquor. Overall, low scrap weight gives high leaching yields of metals, whereas increasing the proportion of scrap leads to incomplete leaching, particularly nickel. The effect of scrap weight on leaching of rare earths seems to be insignificant within the experimental range of scrap weights studied. However, the use of excessively small amounts of scrap is evidently undesirable from the point of view of maximizing metal concentration in the leach liquor and minimizing the lixiviant consumption. Accordingly, the suitable scrap weight was considered to be 5.5 g in 50 ml of acid solution.\nBased on the above experimental results, the final optimum conditions for leaching were determined to be 3 M hydrochloric acid, a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:9 at a temperature of 95 ^ ∘C for 3 h. Under these conditions, 96% of nickel, > 99 % of rare earths and 100% of cobalt could be leached. At the same time, however, the other impurity elements were also nearly completely dissolved in the solution. The average composition of the resulting leach liquor was found to be approximately, in grams per liter: 23.4 Ni, 1.7 Co, 3.4 Fe, 0.72 Zn, 0.46 Al, 1.2 Mn, 4.2 La, 0.26 Ce, 0.82 Pr, 2.6 Nd Ž and 0.074 Sm total RE 7.95 gl ^-1). Separation of impurities and rare earths from cobalt and nickel by solÕent extraction with D2EHPA\nInvestigations into the use of acidic organophosphorus reagents for the solvent extraction of metal ions from aqueous solutions have shown that D2EHPA in organic diluents can be highly loaded with divalent transition metals like Cu ^2+ [ 13 - 17 ], n ^2+ w x 13,16,17, Cd ^2+ w x 15,17, Zn ^2+ w x 2q w x 13,15–17, Co 13,14,16–18, Ni ^2+ 13,14,16,17.w x Moreover, the extractability sequence from chloride medium can be written as Zn ^2+ > Mn ^2+ > Cu ^2+ > Cd ^2+ ≈ C ^2+ > Ni ^2+ 13,17. D2EHPA also exhibits a powerful extrac-w x tion for trivalent metal cations like Fe ^3+ [ 19, 20 ] and Al ^3+ [ 21 - 23 ]. The pH1 / 2 values Ž. defined as the pH at which 50% metal extraction occurs for Zn ^2+, Mn ^2+, F⃗ ⃗e⃗ ⃗^⃗3⃗+⃗ 24, w x Al^3+ 25 lie below pH 3, whereas those of cobalt and nickel are 4.08 and 4.52 24,w x respectively. These data demonstrate the possibility of removing impurities from cobalt and nickel by the use of extraction with D2EHPA at low pH. On the other hand, it is well known that D2EHPA shows an excellent extraction behavior towards trivalent rare earth elements in weakly acidic solution 26,27, and undoubtedly still forms the basis of w x several commercial processes for the separation of these metals 28. Fortunately, thew x separation of the rare earths from these impurities can be achieved by means of selective precipitation with oxalic acid as will be described later.\nFig. 4 gives the results for the extraction of zinc, aluminum, iron, manganese, cobalt, nickel and rare earths with 25 vol.% D2EHPA in kerosene from the actual leach solution mentioned above at various pH values. It is clear that the rare earths can be quantitatively extracted and separated from cobalt and nickel at pH-2.2. However, as expected, under these conditions, nearly complete extraction of aluminum and iron as well as about 85% extraction of zinc takes place. Above pH 2.0, the extraction of cobalt begins to occur. It is noteworthy that, according to the reported data 12,17, manganesew x should be extracted to a considerable extent at pH close to 2. Nevertheless, it can be seen from Fig. 4 that a large amount of rare earths and other impurities such as iron, aluminum and zinc prevent manganese from being taken up into the organic phase, since D2EHPA can extract these metal ions more strongly than manganese. The resulting effect is that only a very small amount of manganese Ž.; 15% is transferred to the organic phase. Hence, it is necessary to increase the organic-to-aqueous ratio and use a multistage extraction operation in order to eliminate manganese completely from the solution. For this reason, the distribution isotherm for the extraction of manganese from the leach liquor by 25% D2EHPA in kerosene was constructed by contacting the two phases at various phase ratios at an equilibrium pH 2.0. The equilibrium data are presented in Fig. 5. The McCable–Thiele diagram indicates that essentially complete removal of manganese can be achieved in two counter-current stages at an organic-toaqueous phase ratio of 3:1. The aqueous feed liquor was therefore processed in a two-stage batch counter-current experiment over six cycles, using 240 ml of organic phase and 80 ml of aqueous phase for each contact. The equilibrium pH for each contact was adjusted to 2.0 with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution. The raffinate obtained after a six-cycle operation, where steady-state conditions had been reached, showed the presence of 0.005 g l ^-1 of manganese. The concentrations of zinc and aluminum were, in g1 ^-1, 0.09 and 0.002, respectively, while those of iron and the rare earths were below\n0.001 gl ^-1.           "text": "## 4. Recovery of cobalt and nickel\nAfter removal of rare earths and impurities from the leach solution by extraction with D2EHPA, the remaining raffinate contained cobalt and nickel as well as a small amount of zinc. In order to recover pure cobalt and nickel products, a cobalt–nickel separation was required. It is known that the selective solvent extraction of cobalt from chloride solutions containing nickel using a tertiary amine extractant is being practiced on a commercial scale 30,31. The extraction of cobalt from an aqueous solution with loww x acidity rises with the chloride ion concentration. Substantial extraction of cobalt occurs at [ C ] ^- ] ≥200 g1 ^-1 32,33. Hence, in the present work, the raffinate was concentratedw x by evaporation to reach a chloride ion concentration of about 220 g1 ^-1 before extraction.\nPreliminary tests on a concentrated aqueous feed liquor showed insufficient extraction of cobalt in a single contact at unit phase ratio with 25% TOA in kerosene. Accordingly, to achieve quantitative extraction of cobalt, the distribution isotherm for the extraction of cobalt from the concentrated solution by 25% TOA in kerosene was determined. The results are shown in Fig. 7. The McCable–Thiele construction demonstrates that it should be possible to achieve nearly complete extraction of cobalt from a solution initially containing 6.75 gl ^-1 of cobalt in three counter-current stages at an O:A ratio of 2:1. To confirm this, a three-stage counter-current batch simulation was carried out. After nine cycles the representative raffinate was found to contain 0.018 g 1 ^-1 of cobalt corresponding to an extraction yield of > 99.7 %. The loaded organic phase contained 3.37 g l ^-1 of cobalt.\nSubsequently the cobalt in the loaded organic phase was stripped by contacting it with a dilute hydrochloric acid solution pH 2.0 in a single stage at an O:A ratio of 4:1. Ž. The stripped organic phase was found to contain only 0.007 g1 ^-1 of cobalt, indicating a stripping efficiency of 99.8%. The strip liquor was a pure cobalt chloride solution containing 13.45 gl ^-1 of cobalt. It should be pointed out, that although zinc has been reported to be extracted from chloride medium by TOA 32,34, no zinc was observed inw x the loaded organic phase in the current work.\nThe cobalt in the strip solution was recovered as a cobalt oxalate precipitate by the addition of an excess of ammonium oxalate. The percentage precipitation of cobalt was over 98.5%.\nThe raffinate from the cobalt extraction contained high levels of nickel, together with a small amount of zinc and trace levels of cobalt. The nickel was recovered directly as a nickel oxalate by precipitation with ammonium oxalate. The contents of impurity elements in the obtained products were determined to be 0.004% cobalt, 0.002% aluminum, 0.098% zinc and < 0.002 % manganese. No iron and rare earth elements were detected by ICP-AES. The average recovery of nickel was higher than 99.9%.",
